clue.text: The big house on the square

definitions.text: The big house on the square

parts.words: The big house on the square
parts.note: a stately home is one sense; the chess piece that moves along rows and files of squares is the other

explanation.surface: A grand mansion overlooking a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'square' is one of the sixty-four on a chessboard, where the piece also called a rook stands.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified stately home and the chess rook share one name.

clue.text: But not 'where Ireland fronts the sea

definitions.text: But not 'where Ireland fronts the sea

parts.words: But not 'where Ireland fronts the sea
parts.note: ire is anger, so a headland of ire-land would be named for anger, but this one is in Scotland, not Ireland

explanation.surface: A coast that is not the Irish shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Read Ireland as 'ire-land': a headland named for ire meets the sea, yet this one is at the north-west tip of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: This headland is a cape on the Scottish coast named with a word for anger.

clue.text: High-lighted

parts.note: given top billing, or lit from high above by stars

explanation.surface: Marked with a highlighter pen.
explanation.walkthrough: Something emphasised or featured as a lead, and also lit from the sky by stars.
explanation.definitionFit: Featured as a lead performer, or marked with an asterisk.

clue.text: Mr. Warner ?

parts.note: a warner is someone who gives warning, like a sentry posted to watch

explanation.surface: A gentleman called Warner, perhaps the cricketer Plum Warner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warner' looks like a surname; it means one who warns.
explanation.definitionFit: A sentry posted to watch for danger is the one who raises the alarm.

clue.text: One that time delves in beauty's brow

definitions.text: One that time delves in beauty's brow

parts.words: One that time delves in beauty's brow
parts.note: Shakespeare's Sonnet 60 says Time 'delves the ... in beauty's brow', meaning digs wrinkles in a forehead

explanation.surface: A line of verse about age wrinkling a lovely face.
explanation.walkthrough: An allusion: the clue quotes Shakespeare's Sonnet 60, where the furrows Time digs in a brow are called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The lines ageing carves across a forehead run side by side, equidistant like the geometric kind.

clue.text: Just awful their battledress, was it said ?

definitions.text: Just awful their battledress, was it said ?

parts.words: Just awful their battledress, was it said ?
parts.note: the alliterative verse begins 'An Austrian army, awfully arrayed', so their battledress was said to be awful

explanation.surface: A complaint about an army's dreadful uniforms.
explanation.walkthrough: An allusion to the old alliterative alphabet rhyme opening 'An Austrian army, awfully arrayed, boldly by battery besieged Belgrade'.
explanation.definitionFit: The soldiers of the old rhyme came from the Habsburg empire centred on Vienna.

clue.text: The devotion to something From the sphere of our sorrow (Shelley)

definitions.text: The devotion to something From the sphere of our sorrow (Shelley)

parts.words: The devotion to something From the sphere of our sorrow (Shelley)
parts.note: a quotation from Shelley's lyric 'One word is too often profaned', with one word left out

explanation.surface: A line of Shelley with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Shelley's line runs 'The devotion to something ___ / From the sphere of our sorrow'; the missing word means at a distance.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means far away, distant from our sorrowful world.

clue.text: Alice out of Wonderland

parts.note: the real girl for whom Lewis Carroll told the story, outside the book

explanation.surface: Alice leaving Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice Liddell, daughter of an Oxford dean, was the real child behind the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's heroine was modelled on the real girl of that surname.

clue.text: He omits two notes of a cradle song

indicators.note: leaving out letters from the song's name

parts.note: a lullaby is a song to rock a cradle to
A and B are two notes of the scale

explanation.surface: A singer leaves out two notes of a bedtime song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'omits' removes A and B from LULLABY; 'He' is the composer Jean-Baptiste Lully.
explanation.definitionFit: Lully was the Italian-born composer at the court of Louis XIV, so a man.

clue.text: Disgraced admiral, honoured soldier

definitions.meaning: Admiral John ..., shot in 1757 for failing to relieve Minorca
Field Marshal Julian ..., victor at Vimy Ridge, made a viscount

explanation.surface: Contrasting fates of a sailor and a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous bearers of the surname: one sailor executed, one general ennobled.

clue.text: 19th-cent, philanthropist — shown up by Podsnap ?

definitions.meaning: George ..., the American banker who funded housing for London's poor
snapping open a pod reveals the body of a pea; Podsnap is also a Dickens character in Our Mutual Friend

explanation.surface: A Victorian benefactor upstaged by a pompous Dickens character.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Podsnap is a smug figure in Dickens; read instead as 'pod-snap', the act that exposes a pea's body inside its shell.
explanation.definitionFit: George Peabody was a famous Victorian benefactor whose trust still houses Londoners.

clue.text: Ill report no impediment to scholarship in this

definitions.text: no impediment to scholarship in this
definitions.meaning: Sheridan's comedy The School for ... shows there can be a school for it, so it does not bar learning

explanation.surface: Gossip that, oddly, does not stop anyone studying.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half alludes to Sheridan's play The School for Scandal: since a school exists for it, it is no bar to scholarship.
explanation.definitionFit: Damaging gossip and public disgrace are the core senses of the word.

clue.text: Scrap merchants

parts.note: a scrap is a fight, and a monger is a dealer, so these are dealers in fighting

explanation.surface: Dealers in scrap metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like junk metal but means a fight; 'merchants' points to the -monger ending.
explanation.definitionFit: People who stir up wars trade in fighting, as a fishmonger trades in fish.

clue.text: Peter the Painter

parts.note: Also the nickname of an anarchist linked to the 1911 Sidney Street siege

explanation.surface: The nickname of a notorious London anarchist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter the Painter' was the nickname of a wanted anarchist in 1911 London, but here it is a real Peter who painted.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Peter Lely was the leading portrait painter of Restoration England.

clue.text: Menagerial decorations?

parts.note: awards for bravery that sound as if they came from a zoo: medals and big cats

explanation.surface: Ornaments for a zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as MEDAL plus LIONS, a decoration from the menagerie; the whole is a round medal-like ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: Large round ornaments or decorations, like oversized medals.

clue.text: He seems willing to hear your account of the business

definitions.text: He seems willing to hear your account of the business

parts.words: He seems willing to hear your account of the business
parts.note: the Latin source word means a listener, and the official examines a firm's accounts

explanation.surface: A patient listener happy to hear how your firm is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' reads as a story told, but means the financial books; the title also comes from Latin for 'hearer'.
explanation.definitionFit: An inspector of company books is literally, from the Latin, a hearer.

clue.text: Granny's not so tight as to go on the rocks at any rate !

definitions.text: Granny's not so tight as to go on the rocks at any rate !

parts.words: Granny's not so tight as to go on the rocks at any rate !
parts.note: a granny knot slips while its correct counterpart holds; reefs are rocks and knots measure speed

explanation.surface: Grandmother is not drunk enough to take whisky on the rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Granny' is the granny knot, the badly tied version; 'tight' means drunk on the surface; reefs are rocks and knots a rate of speed.
explanation.definitionFit: The correct square knot is the one a granny knot fails to be.

clue.text: Classical painter might copy Cot man when his back was turned

parts.note: to ape is to imitate

indicators.note: a turned back signals the painter's name is read from end to start

parts.note: John Sell Cotman, the Norwich watercolourist, whose middle name is Sell

explanation.surface: An ancient artist imitating an English painter behind his back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when his back was turned' reverses SELL, the middle name of John Sell Cotman, giving LLES after APE.
explanation.definitionFit: Apelles was the most celebrated painter of ancient Greece, court artist to Alexander.

clue.text: Implement to connect attic with cellar ?

definitions.text: Implement to connect attic with cellar ?

parts.words: Implement to connect attic with cellar ?
parts.note: Attic salt is a phrase for wit, and the salt cellar is the dish at table

explanation.surface: A tool linking the top of the house to the basement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'attic' and 'cellar' are rooms on the surface; 'Attic salt' means elegant wit, and a salt cellar is a condiment dish.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny spoon for serving salt from a cellar.

clue.text: War minister too late to harry Havelok

parts.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's name for the young Harry, Henry V
Havelok the Dane is the hero of a medieval English romance

explanation.surface: A minister arriving too late to harass a medieval hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'harry' looks like a verb meaning harass; it is Harry, called Hal, followed by the Dane of the romance.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Haldane was Secretary of State for War from 1905 to 1912, reforming the British Army.

clue.text: Jenny, for instance, to render "Auld Robin Gray"?

definitions.text: Jenny, for instance, to render "Auld Robin Gray

parts.note: Jenny Lind, the Swedish soprano
to say is to render or recite

explanation.surface: Asking whether a famous singer would perform an old Scottish ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Anne Lindsay wrote the ballad 'Auld Robin Gray', whose heroine is named Jenny; the clue reads as Lind to say it.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Anne Lindsay was the Scottish poet who wrote the ballad.

clue.text: Improvement on the tomahawk!

parts.note: a sharper blade for scalping than the axe of frontier legend

explanation.surface: A better hatchet.
explanation.walkthrough: The tomahawk is linked in legend with scalping, so the 'improvement' is a surgeon's blade whose name contains scalp.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon's fine knife has a name built on scalp.

clue.text: Swan-feed on the Welsh sands

parts.note: a pen is a female swan
to dine is to feed

explanation.surface: Feeding swans on a Welsh beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Pendine Sands in Carmarthenshire is a long beach used for land speed records.
explanation.definitionFit: Pendine is a Welsh village with seven miles of flat beach.

clue.text: Sea-horse's?

parts.note: white-capped waves are called white horses, and their foaming crests look like flowing neck hair

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the little fish called a sea-horse.
explanation.walkthrough: Not the fish: a breaking wave is a 'white horse', and its spray is the hair on its neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The long neck hair of a horse is pictured on the crest of a wave.

clue.text: That's the idea, to send up a suitable O.M.

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending up reads the letters from the bottom

parts.note: fit means suitable
OM stands for the Order of Merit

explanation.surface: Proposing to honour a deserving recipient of the Order of Merit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to send up' reverses FIT + OM, giving MO TIF.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring theme in art or music is its central idea.

clue.text: Mean they're very fine knappers ?

parts.note: a knapper chips flint into tools; misers are said to be so mean they would peel a flint

explanation.surface: Stingy people who are also expert stoneworkers.
explanation.walkthrough: A knapper shapes flint; a very fine one could peel the skin off it, which is what misers are proverbially said to do to save money.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers proverbially would skin a flint to save a penny.

clue.text: " Quick ones'" ?

parts.note: brief drinks, or rapid pinches

explanation.surface: Fast things.
explanation.walkthrough: A quick one is a swift drink, a small tot of spirits; a pinch is also quick.
explanation.definitionFit: Small measures of spirits, drunk quickly.

clue.text: What a tooth, as the patient did not say

definitions.meaning: an old word for a long pointed tooth, like a horse's canine

definitions.text: as the patient did not say
definitions.meaning: an exclamation of impatience, which a patient person would not utter

explanation.surface: A dentist's patient biting back a remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'patient' looks like the dentist's client; it means a calm person who would not exclaim in irritation.
explanation.definitionFit: A canine tooth, and an old word of irritated dismissal.

clue.text: Shelling over the heads of advancing troops

definitions.text: Shelling over the heads of advancing troops

parts.words: Shelling over the heads of advancing troops
parts.note: Roman soldiers locked shields overhead like a tortoise's shell

explanation.surface: Artillery firing over the infantry as they advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelling' suggests artillery, but it is a shell-like roof of shields that Roman legionaries raised over their heads.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman shield formation was named from the Latin for tortoise.

clue.text: May this publicity man get cross one moment ?

parts.note: a PR man is a pro, short for public relations officer
a cross is written as X
Roman numeral one is I
a mo is a moment

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a press agent will lose his temper briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May' looks like 'might'; it is the month, which in April would be described with this Latin word for next month.
explanation.definitionFit: The old commercial term means of next month, so in April it describes May.

clue.text: August horse-tail ?

parts.note: a horse's tail swishes away insects in late summer, and a tuft of horsehair on a handle does the same job

explanation.surface: A distinguished horse's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'August' looks like the adjective meaning grand; it is the month, when insects plague horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A horsehair swat on a handle is used to drive off insects.

clue.text: North star contrariwise is in our wake

indicators.note: the two pieces are taken in the opposite order to the clue's

parts.note: aster is the Greek word for star, as in asterisk

explanation.surface: The Pole Star seen behind a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrariwise' swaps the order, so ASTER comes before N.
explanation.definitionFit: Behind a ship is where its wake trails.
